case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act bars civil liability when an online platform’s recommendation algorithms amplify and suggest third-party terrorist content to users, or whether that conduct can be treated as the platform’s own actionable conduct outside Section 230’s immunity (and/or as aiding-and-abetting under the Anti-Terrorism Act).
case_analysis.legal_provision: 47 U.S.C. § 230(c)(1) (Communications Decency Act immunity for interactive computer services); related merits backdrop: 18 U.S.C. § 2333(d) (Anti-Terrorism Act/JASTA aiding-and-abetting liability).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (family members of a victim of an ISIS attack) argue that Google/YouTube is not merely hosting third-party ISIS videos but is affirmatively recommending and amplifying them through algorithms designed to increase engagement; that recommending content is Google’s own conduct and/or its own ‘information content’ in relevant part, so the suit does not treat Google as the publisher or speaker of another’s content in the way Section 230 protects. They contend Section 230 was meant to protect traditional editorial functions like hosting, removing, or organizing user content, not targeted recommendations that materially contribute to harm, and that allowing immunity here would create a sweeping shield even when platforms actively steer users toward terrorist propaganda. They further maintain that this recommendation conduct can support Anti-Terrorism Act aiding-and-abetting theories (at least as a legal sufficiency matter at the pleading stage), because amplification and matching can substantially assist terrorist entities by increasing reach, recruitment, and operational support.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Google argues the claims inherently seek to hold YouTube liable for decisions about displaying, arranging, and recommending third-party videos—classic publisher functions protected by Section 230. In Google’s view, algorithmic recommendations are an inseparable part of publishing at internet scale (ranking, sorting, and suggesting content), and imposing liability would effectively treat platforms as speakers of user content, contrary to the statute’s text and purpose. Google also contends petitioners’ theory would expose platforms to massive, unpredictable liability for ordinary content curation tools used across the internet, chilling online speech and forcing over-removal. On the ATA/JASTA backdrop, Google disputes that the complaint plausibly alleges the necessary elements of aiding-and-abetting (e.g., knowing and substantial assistance), characterizing the alleged conduct as generalized platform availability and neutral tools rather than purposeful support of ISIS.
key_precedents: Zeran v. America Online, Inc., 129 F.3d 327 (4th Cir. 1997) (early broad construction of Section 230 immunity)
Fair Housing Council of San Fernando Valley v. Roommates.com, LLC, 521 F.3d 1157 (9th Cir. 2008) (en banc) (limits on Section 230 when a service materially contributes to unlawful content)
Force v. Facebook, Inc., 934 F.3d 53 (2d Cir. 2019) (Section 230 applied to recommendation/matching features in terrorism-related claims; note the split/criticism in dissents)
Dyroff v. Ultimate Software Group, Inc., 934 F.3d 1093 (9th Cir. 2019) (Section 230 immunity for recommendations/notifications tied to user content)
Gonzalez v. Google LLC, 2 F.4th 871 (9th Cir. 2021) (decision below applying Section 230 to the recommendation claims)
Twitter, Inc. v. Taamneh, 598 U.S. 471 (2023) (clarified ATA aiding-and-abetting standards; decided in the companion case context)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is that “affirmative” recommendations can be characterized as the platform’s own steering conduct, but under § 230(c)(1) the dispositive question is whether the claim would treat the service as a publisher of information provided by another—and selecting, arranging, and presenting third-party speech (even via algorithms) is the modern form of publishing. As Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett emphasize, Roommates.com’s “material contribution” limit is triggered when the service helps develop the unlawful aspect of the content; a generally applicable recommendation tool applied to already-unlawful ISIS videos does not plausibly make the platform a co-developer of the illegality. The lower-court line Justice Alito notes (Zeran, Force, Dyroff) reinforces that a recommendation carveout would be a judicially invented, hard-to-administer exception with broad chilling effects—an institutional-legitimacy concern better addressed by Congress. Taamneh further supports resolving any culpable-amplification concerns through ATA/JASTA’s demanding knowing-and-substantial-assistance standard rather than by narrowing § 230 in this case.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s “affirmative steering” framing is the best case for petitioner, but under the ordinary public meaning of “publisher” in § 230(c)(1), selecting, arranging, and presenting third-party material—including by automated recommendation—is quintessential publication activity, so imposing liability for that conduct necessarily “treat[s]” the service as the publisher of “information provided by another.” As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan explain, Roommates.com’s “material contribution” limit is triggered when the service helps develop the unlawful aspect of the content itself; here, the alleged unlawfulness inheres in ISIS’s videos, and a generally applicable ranking tool does not make Google an “information content provider” of that illegality. Justice Sotomayor’s concern that this collapses § 230 whenever algorithms are used is a policy argument better directed to Congress; the text contains no administrable host/recommend line that would exclude ordinary editorial functions at scale. Taamneh further confirms that, even apart from § 230, these allegations of generalized recommendation features do not plausibly plead knowing and substantial assistance tied to the specific terrorist act.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s reframing of recommendations as the platform’s “affirmative conduct” does not overcome § 230(c)(1)’s text, because the only way her theory generates liability is by treating YouTube as a publisher for its selection, arrangement, and presentation of “information provided by another.” As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas emphasize, those are classic publisher functions in ordinary meaning, and automation does not change their character. Roommates.com’s “material contribution” limit is not plausibly triggered here because, as Justice Barrett notes, the complaint does not allege YouTube developed the unlawful aspect of ISIS’s content; it alleges distribution and prioritization using generally applicable tools. Finally, Taamneh—invoked by several colleagues—confirms that generalized recommendation features, without well-pleaded knowing and substantial assistance tied to the specific terrorist act, are a poor fit for aiding-and-abetting liability and do not justify narrowing § 230 in this case.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s best point is that recommending and ranking are modern forms of editorial discretion covered by § 230 as read in Zeran and reflected in Force and Dyroff, and I take seriously his administrability and chilling-effect concerns. But that argument risks reading “publisher” so capaciously that any algorithmic steering—no matter how intentionally designed to push users toward illegal material—becomes categorically immune, even when the complaint targets the platform’s own conduct (the design and deployment of an amplification system) rather than liability for the underlying third-party words. Justice Kagan is right that Roommates.com’s “material contribution” is clearest when the platform helps develop the illegality of the content, yet I read it more functionally: when a platform’s system plausibly contributes to the wrongful dissemination in a way that is more than passive display—especially alleged targeted promotion to susceptible users—the pleading should not be dismissed as merely treating the platform “as the publisher” of ISIS’s information. Taamneh may well doom petitioners on scienter/substantial assistance later, but it does not justify expanding § 230 at the threshold to foreclose inquiry into real-world amplification harms that the platform itself allegedly drives.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to press that algorithmic “recommendations” can feel like affirmative steering, and if § 230 turned on intuitive moral salience I might worry about giving platforms a blanket pass. But under the text—liability that would “treat” the service “as the publisher or speaker” of “information provided by another”—the gravamen here is still YouTube’s selection, arrangement, and display of ISIS’s third‑party videos, which Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett persuasively frame as quintessential publishing functions even when automated. Roommates.com’s “material contribution” limit does real work, but as Justice Thomas notes it targets situations where the service helps develop the unlawful aspect of the content; a generally applicable engagement-based ranking tool applied to already-unlawful third-party material does not plausibly cross that line on these pleadings. And Taamneh’s demanding knowing/substantial-assistance framework underscores that petitioners’ amplification concerns fit better as merits limits under ATA/JASTA than as atextual narrowing of § 230 in this case.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best argument is that targeted recommendations are the platform’s own affirmative conduct, but § 230(c)(1) asks whether the cause of action would “treat” the service “as the publisher or speaker” of “information provided by another,” and—as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas stress—selection, arrangement, and presentation of third-party speech (whether by humans or automation) is the core publishing function. Roommates.com’s “material contribution” limit does not fit here because, unlike structuring users’ illegal responses, the platform is not alleged to have created, required, or developed the unlawful aspect of ISIS’s videos; using a generally applicable engagement-ranking tool does not make YouTube an “information content provider” of the ISIS content. The lower-court line Roberts cites (Zeran; Force; Dyroff) does not bind us, but it confirms the ordinary, administrable reading of the statute’s text and cautions against a judicially invented “recommendation” carveout lacking a textual hook. And as Justice Kagan and others note, Taamneh’s demanding knowing-and-substantial-assistance standard makes this case a poor vehicle to rework § 230 when the more natural place to test culpable amplification is on ATA/JASTA merits.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point remains that affirmative, engagement-driven recommendations can look like the platform’s own steering rather than passive hosting, and she invokes Roommates.com’s “material contribution” limit. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, the liability theory still necessarily treats YouTube “as the publisher” of “information provided by another” because the alleged wrong is the organization, prioritization, and presentation of third-party ISIS videos—functions that fit the ordinary, historically grounded understanding of publishing, whether done by humans or algorithms. Roommates.com is meaningfully different because the service there structured and required illegal content inputs; here the platform is not alleged to have developed the unlawful aspect of the videos, and converting neutral recommendation/ranking into “material contribution” lacks a textual hook and would be unadministrable. Taamneh further supports resolving this case without narrowing § 230 because the pleadings’ generalized-tool theory also struggles to meet knowing-and-substantial-assistance standards on the merits.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is that algorithmic recommendations are “affirmative conduct” that can be characterized as the platform’s own steering, but § 230(c)(1)’s text asks whether the claim would treat the service “as the publisher or speaker” of “information provided by another,” and—as the Chief Justice and Justice Thomas stress—selection, arrangement, and presentation of others’ speech are ordinary publishing functions, whether done by humans or automated tools. Roommates.com’s “material contribution” limit, invoked by Justice Sotomayor, does not fit these pleadings because the alleged unlawfulness inheres in ISIS’s videos, not in YouTube’s development of their illegal content; a generally applicable engagement-based ranking tool does not plausibly make YouTube an “information content provider” of that content. The lower-court line Chief Justice Roberts cites (Zeran; Force; Dyroff) reinforces this original-meaning reading and underscores the administrability problems of a recommendation carveout without a textual hook. Taamneh further confirms that plaintiffs’ theory sounds in generalized amplification rather than knowing, substantial assistance tied to specific terrorist acts, making this a poor vehicle to narrow § 230.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is that algorithmic “recommendations” can be experienced as affirmative steering and thus as the platform’s own conduct, which raises real fairness and harm concerns at the pleading stage. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan stress, § 230(c)(1) asks whether the claim would “treat” the service as the publisher of information provided by another, and the alleged wrong here remains inseparable from arranging and presenting third-party ISIS videos—an editorial function even when automated. Roommates.com does not undermine that conclusion on these allegations because, as Justice Barrett notes, there is no plausible claim that YouTube materially contributed to the unlawfulness of the content itself (by requiring, inducing, or shaping the illegal aspect), as opposed to using a generally applicable ranking tool. Taamneh, highlighted by Justice Kavanaugh, further reinforces the pragmatic concern that narrowing § 230 in this vehicle would likely produce broad chilling effects without actually fitting the demanding knowing-and-substantial-assistance framework that would make liability sensible on the merits.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 230(c)(1) bars claims that would hold an interactive computer service liable “as the publisher or speaker” of third-party content, and algorithmic ranking and recommendation are, at the relevant level of generality, part of the platform’s traditional editorial function of organizing and displaying others’ speech. Consistent with Zeran’s broad reading of § 230 and the substantial weight of lower-court authority applying immunity to recommendations (e.g., Force v. Facebook; Dyroff; and the Ninth Circuit’s decision below in Gonzalez), imposing liability here would risk sweeping, speech-chilling consequences and invite courts to supervise ordinary content curation at internet scale—an institutional-legitimacy concern best left to Congress to recalibrate. Roommates.com’s “material contribution” limitation is not satisfied on these pleadings where the alleged unlawfulness lies in ISIS’s videos themselves, not in Google creating or developing the illicit content; the recommendation tools are neutral and operate on third-party material. Any further relief can proceed, if at all, under the ATA/JASTA standards clarified in Twitter v. Taamneh, but § 230 still forecloses treating YouTube’s recommendations of third-party videos as actionable publication decisions.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of § 230(c)(1) bars treating an interactive computer service “as the publisher or speaker of any information provided by another information content provider,” and recommendation/ranking is best understood as part of the publisher’s function of selecting and presenting third-party material at scale rather than the platform’s own “information.” See 47 U.S.C. § 230(c)(1); Zeran v. AOL, 129 F.3d 327, 332–33 (4th Cir. 1997). While Roommates.com recognizes § 230’s limit where the service “materially contributes” to the unlawfulness of the content, merely using neutral algorithms to sort and suggest third-party videos does not plausibly make the platform a co-developer of ISIS’s message. 521 F.3d 1157 (9th Cir. 2008) (en banc). And under Taamneh’s demanding aiding-and-abetting standards, generalized recommendation tools without knowing and substantial assistance to ISIS are insufficient on the ATA theory. 598 U.S. 471 (2023).

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 230(c)(1) bars claims that would treat an interactive computer service as the “publisher or speaker” of information provided by another, and algorithmic ranking and recommendation are modern means of the same publishing functions—selecting, arranging, and presenting third-party content—at internet scale. Consistent with Force v. Facebook and Dyroff, imposing liability because YouTube’s systems suggested ISIS-produced videos would necessarily hinge on YouTube’s dissemination decisions regarding third-party content, which § 230 protects. Roommates.com’s “material contribution” limitation is not satisfied where the platform did not create or develop the unlawful content itself, but used neutral tools to organize and surface user-provided material. And under Taamneh’s demanding ATA/JASTA aiding-and-abetting standard, generalized recommendations and availability of standard platform features do not plausibly establish the knowing and substantial assistance required, especially given the practical consequences of exposing ubiquitous curation tools to massive liability.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 230(c)(1) bars treating a platform as the “publisher or speaker” of third-party information, but an affirmative, targeted recommendation system that amplifies and steers users toward terrorist content can be characterized as the platform’s own actionable conduct rather than mere hosting or editorial judgment. Under Roommates.com, Section 230 has limits where the service “materially contributes” to the unlawfulness, and algorithmic amplification designed to increase engagement plausibly crosses from neutral organization into conduct that contributes to harmful dissemination. At minimum, the complaint should not be dismissed at the pleading stage where petitioners allege recommendation tools that promote ISIS propaganda to susceptible users, implicating real-world harms to vulnerable populations and warranting judicial scrutiny rather than categorical immunity. Separately, in light of Taamneh’s emphasis on knowing and substantial assistance under 18 U.S.C. § 2333(d), the amplification allegations may still face a demanding merits standard, but Section 230 should not foreclose consideration where the platform’s own recommendation conduct is the gravamen.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 230(c)(1) bars claims that would "treat[]" an interactive computer service "as the publisher or speaker" of third-party information, and algorithmic recommendation/ranking is best understood as a modern form of the editorial judgment inherent in publication at scale. Under the Roommates.com “material contribution” limit, immunity is lost when the platform helps develop the unlawfulness of the content itself (e.g., by requiring or shaping illegal content), but recommending existing third-party videos—without plausibly alleging that Google created or materially contributed to their illegal character—looks closer to protected curation than to content development. Consistent with Force v. Facebook and Dyroff, imposing liability for neutral recommendation tools would effectively attach publisher liability to the dissemination/arrangement of others’ speech, undermining statutory coherence and workability across the internet. And in light of Twitter v. Taamneh’s emphasis on knowing and substantial assistance, petitioners’ aiding-and-abetting theory (as pleaded) is better addressed on ATA merits than by narrowing §230 to carve out routine recommendation functions absent a clear textual hook.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 230(c)(1) provides that no provider of an interactive computer service shall be treated as the publisher or speaker of information provided by another, and algorithmic sorting and recommending of third-party videos is best understood as a modern form of the traditional editorial judgment inherent in publication. On that reading, petitioners’ theory still seeks to impose liability for YouTube’s dissemination and arrangement of ISIS-created content, which § 230 bars as construed in Zeran and applied to recommendation features in Force and Dyroff. Roommates.com’s “material contribution” limit is not satisfied where the platform did not require or develop the unlawful content itself, but instead used generally applicable recommendation tools to display user content. And to the extent petitioners rely on aiding-and-abetting under 18 U.S.C. § 2333(d), Taamneh underscores the need for knowing and substantial assistance, which is not plausibly shown by neutral, widely available recommendation mechanisms alone.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 230(c)(1) bars claims that would treat an interactive computer service “as the publisher or speaker” of third-party content, and algorithmic ranking and recommendation are, in practical operation, part of the core editorial function of organizing and presenting that content at internet scale. The dominant lower-court precedent has applied § 230 to recommendation and matching features, including Force v. Facebook and Dyroff, and I would be reluctant to upset that settled understanding absent clearer statutory direction from Congress, particularly given the significant workability and chilling-speech concerns. Roommates.com’s “material contribution” limitation does not fit well here because the illegality alleged resides in the third-party ISIS videos, not in content that Google itself required or created. And in light of Twitter v. Taamneh’s demanding standards for ATA/JASTA aiding-and-abetting (knowing, substantial assistance tied to the specific wrongdoing), the complaint’s allegations about generalized recommendation tools are unlikely to plausibly cross that threshold in any event, reinforcing that this is not an appropriate vehicle to narrow § 230.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 230(c)(1) bars claims that would “treat” an interactive computer service “as the publisher or speaker” of “information provided by another information content provider,” and the ordinary, common-law understanding of publishing includes the editorial functions of selecting, organizing, and presenting others’ speech—functions that, at internet scale, are performed through ranking and recommendation algorithms. Courts have consistently read § 230(c)(1) to cover liability theories predicated on these publication decisions, including in Zeran v. AOL and later in Force v. Facebook and Dyroff, which treated recommendations and matching features as publisher conduct with respect to third-party content. Petitioners do not plausibly allege that YouTube itself “develop[ed]” the ISIS content so as to become an “information content provider” under § 230(f)(3), as Roommates.com requires for the “material contribution” exception, and Taamneh’s demanding ATA/JASTA aiding-and-abetting standard underscores that generalized algorithmic amplification, without well-pleaded knowing and substantial assistance, cannot supply an end-run around § 230’s text. Accordingly, the complaint’s recommendation-based theory seeks to impose liability for how YouTube disseminated others’ information, which § 230(c)(1) forecloses.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 230(c)(1) bars claims that would treat an interactive computer service as the publisher of “information provided by another information content provider,” and the pleaded theory here targets YouTube’s ranking and recommendation of third-party ISIS videos—functions that multiple circuits have treated as paradigmatic publication activity at internet scale. While Roommates.com recognizes a limit when the service “materially contributes” to the unlawfulness of content, 521 F.3d at 1168, an engagement-optimizing recommendation algorithm that does not itself require or induce unlawful content is more like the neutral matching tools held immune in Force v. Facebook and Dyroff. Given Taamneh’s demanding “knowing and substantial assistance” standard for ATA aiding-and-abetting, the complaint’s generalized allegations about amplification via ubiquitous recommendation tools do not plausibly allege the requisite culpable participation, and expanding liability here would create serious practical chilling and over-removal consequences inconsistent with § 230’s design.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Section 230(c)(1) of the Communications Decency Act immunizes Google/YouTube from civil liability under the Anti-Terrorism Act for allegedly recommending ISIS-related videos to users through algorithmic recommendations, as distinct from merely hosting third-party content.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 47 U.S.C. § 230(c)(1) (Communications Decency Act § 230) (with the underlying cause of action arising under the Anti-Terrorism Act, 18 U.S.C. § 2333, as amended by JASTA, Pub. L. 114-222).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (family members of an ISIS terror victim) argue that YouTube’s targeted algorithmic recommendations are YouTube’s own affirmative conduct—effectively promoting and amplifying ISIS content to users—and therefore fall outside Section 230’s immunity, which they contend protects only passive publishing/hosting of third-party content. They maintain that their claims do not treat Google as the ‘publisher or speaker’ of another’s content in the traditional sense; rather, Google’s recommendation systems are independent product features that materially contribute to the alleged wrongful act (aiding-and-abetting terrorism under the ATA/JASTA) by matching ISIS content to susceptible audiences. Petitioners urge the Court to draw a line between neutral hosting/search functions and platform-driven recommendations that prioritize and push content.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Google argues that recommendations are an ordinary and inseparable part of ‘publishing’ third-party content online (organizing, ranking, and displaying content to users), so claims attacking recommendations necessarily treat Google as the publisher of information provided by another content provider and are therefore barred by Section 230(c)(1). Google contends that holding platforms liable for algorithmic ranking/recommendation would effectively nullify Section 230’s core protection, because all modern services use algorithms to sort and present vast amounts of user-generated content. Google also disputes that the complaint plausibly establishes the elements of ATA/JASTA aiding-and-abetting liability (including knowing and substantial assistance) based on generalized allegations about ISIS content appearing on YouTube.
key_precedents: Zeran v. America Online, Inc., 129 F.3d 327 (4th Cir. 1997)
Fair Housing Council of San Fernando Valley v. Roommates.com, LLC, 521 F.3d 1157 (9th Cir. 2008) (en banc)
Force v. Facebook, Inc., 934 F.3d 53 (2d Cir. 2019)
Dyroff v. Ultimate Software Group, Inc., 934 F.3d 1093 (9th Cir. 2019)
Fields v. Twitter, Inc., 881 F.3d 739 (9th Cir. 2018)
Gonzalez v. Google LLC, 2 F.4th 871 (9th Cir. 2021)

John Roberts.reasoning: The strongest petitioner point remains that algorithmic “recommendations” are affirmative platform conduct, but as Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, the ordinary meaning and common-law backdrop of “publisher” include selecting, arranging, and presenting others’ material—precisely what ranking and recommendation systems do at scale. I also agree with Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor that drawing a hosting-versus-recommending line would be unstable and threaten §230’s core operation, absent a Roommates.com-style allegation that the platform materially contributed to the unlawfulness of the content itself, which is not plausibly pleaded here. Taamneh further supports resolving the case narrowly: even setting §230 aside, generalized allegations about a ubiquitous recommendation system do not plausibly show knowing and substantial assistance tied to the specific attack. A minimalist disposition would affirm on §230(c)(1) and, in the alternative, note that the pleadings fail under Taamneh’s aiding-and-abetting standard without announcing a broad rule about all algorithms.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The petitioners’ best point remains that “recommendations” are affirmative platform conduct—perhaps even the platform’s own speech—rather than “publishing,” but that characterization cannot overcome §230(c)(1)’s text, which bars claims that would treat a service “as the publisher or speaker” of information “provided by another,” and the ordinary 1996 meaning of “publisher” included selection, arrangement, and dissemination. Justice Gorsuch’s emphasis on the common-law backdrop confirms that these are paradigmatic publisher functions, and algorithmic ranking is simply the automated form of the same activity, not a textual carveout. Justice Barrett correctly notes that Roommates.com’s “material contribution” limit turns on the service’s role in developing the unlawful content itself; on these pleadings, YouTube did not require, induce, or create ISIS content, it allegedly displayed it. Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance on Taamneh further reinforces that even apart from §230, generalized allegations about ubiquitous recommendation systems do not plausibly satisfy JASTA’s knowing-and-substantial-assistance standard tied to the specific attack.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The petitioners’ best point remains that “recommendations” look like affirmative platform conduct, but that label does not change what the claim seeks to do: impose liability for selecting, arranging, and presenting third-party speech, which §230(c)(1) bars by forbidding treatment of the service “as the publisher or speaker” of information provided by another. Justice Thomas’s ordinary-meaning framing is decisive for a textualist: in 1996, “publishing” encompassed editorial judgment about what to display and how, and algorithmic ranking is simply that function at scale, not a distinct statutory category. Justice Kagan and the Chief Justice are also right on workability and consequences—carving out recommendations would effectively gut §230 for modern platforms because almost all dissemination now involves prioritization. Even apart from §230, Taamneh’s demanding “knowing and substantial assistance” standard confirms these generalized allegations about ubiquitous recommendation systems do not plausibly state JASTA aiding-and-abetting liability tied to the specific attack.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The strongest petitioner point remains that recommendations feel like affirmative promotion, and as a practical matter they can amplify harmful content in ways that plain hosting does not—an effect that matters for vulnerable communities. But Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan persuasively explain that the liability theory here still “treats” YouTube as a publisher based on how it selects and presents third-party ISIS videos, and carving out recommendations would be unworkable because modern platforms necessarily organize content through ranking and matching. Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch’s ordinary-meaning/common-law account of “publishing” (selection, arrangement, dissemination) reinforces that §230’s text lacks a stable hook for the hosting/recommendation distinction absent a Roommates.com-style allegation that YouTube materially contributed to the videos’ unlawful content. Even setting §230 aside, Taamneh’s requirement of knowing and substantial assistance tied to the specific attack makes these generalized algorithm allegations too attenuated to sustain JASTA aiding-and-abetting liability.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The best petitioner point remains that “recommendations” look like affirmative platform conduct—closer to promotion than passive hosting—but that still seeks to impose liability for how YouTube selects and presents third-party ISIS videos, which is exactly what §230(c)(1) prevents by barring claims that would “treat” the service as the publisher of information “provided by another.” Justice Gorsuch’s common-law framing is especially persuasive to me: publishing historically includes selection, arrangement, and dissemination, and an algorithm is just a scalable way to perform those editorial functions, not a textual carveout from the statute. Roommates.com supplies a principled limit (material contribution to the unlawfulness), but as Justice Barrett emphasizes, these allegations do not plausibly claim YouTube helped develop the illegality of ISIS content; they challenge distribution and prioritization. Finally, even putting §230 aside, Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance on Taamneh highlights that generalized, platform-wide recommendation allegations are too attenuated to plead “knowing and substantial assistance” tied to this attack, and I see no workable, text-grounded way to create a recommendations exception here without Congress.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Petitioners’ best point remains that “recommendations” are affirmative conduct by the platform, arguably distinct from “publishing,” but that contention still seeks to impose liability for selecting, arranging, and disseminating third-party “information”—conduct that, in ordinary legal usage at enactment and at common law, falls within the publisher function §230(c)(1) addresses. Justice Thomas’s emphasis on the 1996 ordinary meaning of “publisher,” echoed by Chief Justice Roberts’s workability concerns, reinforces that we lack a textual basis to carve out algorithmic ranking as categorically different from editorial presentation. Roommates.com, as Justice Barrett notes, supplies a limiting principle only where the service materially contributes to the unlawfulness of the content itself; these allegations target distribution and prioritization of ISIS-created videos, not the development of their illegality. And even if §230’s boundary were debatable, Taamneh’s “knowing and substantial assistance” standard makes this complaint’s generalized allegations about a neutral recommendation system too attenuated to state JASTA aiding-and-abetting liability.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The petitioners’ best point remains that algorithmic recommendations are affirmative platform conduct—akin to targeted promotion—rather than “publishing,” but that distinction collapses under the ordinary 1996 meaning of “publisher,” which (as Justice Thomas emphasizes) included selecting, arranging, and presenting others’ speech. Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance on Force and Dyroff is persuasive institutional evidence that the settled lower-court understanding treats ranking and matching tools as §230(c)(1) functions absent Roommates.com-style “material contribution” to the unlawfulness, which is not plausibly alleged here. Carving out recommendations would create an unstable, unadministrable line that threatens §230’s core operation for modern platforms, a practical concern consistent with maintaining the Court’s legitimacy and adhering to congressional design. And even apart from §230, Taamneh’s demanding knowing-and-substantial-assistance standard cautions against allowing generalized allegations about ubiquitous algorithms to substitute for a tight nexus to the specific attack.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The petitioners’ best point—that algorithmic recommendations are affirmative platform conduct rather than “publishing”—still fails on the statutory text: a claim that targets selection, ordering, and prioritized display of third-party videos necessarily treats the service “as the publisher or speaker” of information “provided by another.” Justice Thomas’s focus on ordinary 1996 meaning and Justice Gorsuch’s common-law backdrop (including Stratton Oakmont) strengthen my view that editorial discretion—whether executed by human judgment or automated rules—falls within the publisher function § 230(c)(1) protects, absent Roommates.com-style material contribution to the content’s illegality. Justice Kagan and the Chief Justice persuasively emphasize workability: a recommendations carveout would be unstable because modern platforms inevitably curate through ranking and matching, and the pleadings here do not allege inducement or development of ISIS content. Even setting § 230 aside, Taamneh’s “knowing and substantial assistance” requirement underscores that generalized allegations about ubiquitous recommendation systems lack the necessary nexus to the specific attack.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The petitioners’ strongest point—that algorithmic recommendations are affirmative “promotion” rather than passive hosting—still ultimately seeks to impose liability for YouTube’s selection, arrangement, and display of third-party ISIS content, which § 230(c)(1) bars by preventing claims that treat a service as the “publisher or speaker” of information provided by another. Justice Kagan’s workability concern is particularly persuasive: trying to carve out “recommendations” would force courts to draw unstable lines among ubiquitous curation tools, with sweeping practical consequences absent clear congressional guidance. Justice Barrett’s and Justice Gorsuch’s reliance on Roommates.com’s “material contribution” limit does not move this case because the pleadings do not plausibly allege Google helped develop the unlawfulness of ISIS videos; they allege dissemination and prioritization. Finally, Chief Justice Roberts’s point about Taamneh reinforces that even if § 230 were uncertain at the margins, these generalized allegations do not plausibly plead knowing and substantial assistance tied to the specific attack.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 230(c)(1) bars claims that would treat an interactive computer service as the “publisher or speaker” of information provided by another, and most courts have understood ordinary ranking and recommendation functions as part of publishing that third-party content rather than the platform’s own content creation. Force v. Facebook and Dyroff held that algorithmic recommendations (including friend/group or content matching) are publisher functions protected by § 230 when they operate on third-party material, and this case can be resolved on that narrow, precedent-consistent ground without rewriting § 230. Roommates.com’s “material contribution” exception is best read to apply where the platform helps develop unlawful content itself, not where it uses neutral tools to display others’ videos. Separately, Taamneh underscores the demanding “knowing and substantial assistance” standard for ATA/JASTA aiding-and-abetting claims, reinforcing the institutional-legitimacy value of avoiding an expansive new liability theory that would destabilize settled § 230 doctrine absent clear congressional direction.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Section 230(c)(1) bars any claim that would “treat[]” an interactive computer service “as the publisher or speaker” of “information provided by another information content provider,” 47 U.S.C. § 230(c)(1); in ordinary legal usage at the time of enactment, a publisher’s functions included deciding whether and how to disseminate, arrange, and present third-party content, which is what algorithmic ranking and recommendation do. Petitioners’ theory still predicates liability on YouTube’s dissemination and prioritization of ISIS-created videos—i.e., publisher-like presentation of another’s information—rather than on YouTube’s creation of the unlawful content itself, and thus falls within the statutory bar as most courts have understood it. Whatever the merits of narrowing § 230 as a policy matter, a textualist reading does not justify carving out “recommendations” from publishing when they are simply a means of selecting and displaying third-party material; any change should come from Congress, not this Court. Taamneh underscores the demanding nature of ATA/JASTA aiding-and-abetting liability and counsels against expanding civil liability based on generalized allegations about platform features, reinforcing that this claim is not plausibly distinct from treating the defendant as a publisher of third-party speech.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 230(c)(1) bars claims that would treat an interactive computer service as the “publisher or speaker” of information “provided by another information content provider,” and algorithmic recommendations are best understood as a modern means of organizing and presenting third-party content—core publishing functions rather than the platform’s own speech. Consistent with Zeran v. AOL’s broad reading of “publisher” liability, and with cases like Force v. Facebook and Dyroff v. Ultimate Software holding that ranking/recommending user content remains within §230, petitioners’ theory would expose platforms to liability whenever they sort content for users, a practical result Congress sought to avoid. Even aside from §230, Twitter v. Taamneh underscores the demanding nature of ATA/JASTA aiding-and-abetting (knowing and substantial assistance), and generalized allegations about ISIS material appearing and being recommended on YouTube do not plausibly establish that level of culpable assistance. The text and the practical consequences both favor immunity here.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 230(c)(1) bars claims that would treat an interactive computer service “as the publisher or speaker” of third-party information, and YouTube’s algorithmic recommendations—however automated and tailored—are best understood as a modern form of organizing and displaying user-generated content. Decisions like Force v. Facebook and Dyroff v. Ultimate Software have treated recommendation, ranking, and notification features as publisher functions protected by §230 when the platform is not alleged to have created or developed the unlawful content itself. Roommates.com’s “material contribution” exception does not fit these allegations absent a showing that YouTube required, induced, or helped develop ISIS content in the way Roommates induced discriminatory preferences, and Taamneh further cautions against expanding ATA/JASTA aiding-and-abetting liability without plausible allegations of knowing and substantial assistance tied to the specific attack. Given Congress’s broad immunity language and the risk that carving out recommendations would swallow §230’s core protection for how platforms present third-party speech at scale, I would affirm immunity here.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 230(c)(1) bars claims that would treat an interactive computer service as the “publisher or speaker” of third-party information, and algorithmic recommendations are best understood—textually and practically—as a form of organizing and presenting that third-party content to users. The complaint targets YouTube’s matching and display of ISIS videos created by others, not Google’s creation or “development” of unlawful content in the Roommates.com sense (where the platform required and structured discriminatory inputs), so Google is not an “information content provider” under § 230(f)(3). Consistent with Zeran and the dominant lower-court approach reflected in Force and Dyroff, imposing ATA/JASTA liability on recommendations would collapse § 230’s core protection for modern content-sorting tools and create unworkable line-drawing between “hosting” and “recommending.” And in any event, Taamneh underscores the demanding “knowing and substantial assistance” requirement for aiding-and-abetting under the ATA, which generalized allegations about the presence of ISIS content and platform-wide recommendation systems do not plausibly satisfy.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 230(c)(1) bars treating an “interactive computer service” as the “publisher or speaker” of information “provided by another information content provider,” and, at common law, “publishing” encompassed editorial choices about organizing, selecting, and distributing others’ speech—functions closely aligned with algorithmic ranking and recommendations. The history Congress had in view, including Stratton Oakmont v. Prodigy, confirms that “publisher” liability turned on exercising editorial control, and §230 was enacted to prevent imposing that liability on online services for third-party content. While Roommates.com recognizes a limit where the platform materially contributes to unlawfulness as an information content provider, recommending third-party ISIS videos does not itself create or develop the illegal content alleged, and imposing ATA/JASTA aiding-and-abetting liability on these publication-like choices would effectively circumvent §230(c)(1). In any event, Taamneh underscores the demanding requirements of knowing and substantial assistance under JASTA, which generalized allegations about recommendations struggle to satisfy.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 230(c)(1) bars claims that would treat an interactive computer service as the “publisher or speaker” of third-party information, and longstanding precedent has construed “publisher” broadly to include core editorial functions such as organizing, presenting, and disseminating others’ content. Under Zeran v. America Online, Inc., § 230 precludes liability premised on decisions about whether and how to display third-party speech, and lower courts (e.g., Force v. Facebook; Dyroff) have treated algorithmic ranking/recommendation as an ordinary means of publishing at internet scale rather than the platform’s creation of the underlying content. Petitioners’ ATA/JASTA theory still targets Google’s dissemination and prioritization of ISIS-created videos—information “provided by another information content provider”—and expanding liability for algorithmic recommendations would create serious practical and workability problems inconsistent with § 230’s text and structure. Separately, Taamneh underscores the demanding nature of aiding-and-abetting liability (knowing and substantial assistance), reinforcing judicial restraint in extending novel liability here absent clearer congressional direction.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 230(c)(1) bars treating an “interactive computer service” as the “publisher or speaker” of “information provided by another information content provider,” and algorithmic recommendations are best understood—as a matter of ordinary meaning and settled lower-court practice—as a quintessential publishing function (organizing, selecting, and presenting third-party content), not the platform’s creation or “development” of the underlying information. Unlike Roommates.com, where the platform materially contributed to illegality by requiring and structuring unlawful content, the complaint here targets YouTube’s distribution and prioritization of ISIS videos created by others, which falls within the publisher-liability core recognized in Zeran and applied to recommendation features in Force and Dyroff. Methodological consistency and respect for widespread precedent favor applying § 230 absent plausible allegations that YouTube itself became an “information content provider” under § 230(f)(3) by materially contributing to the content’s unlawfulness. Separately, Taamneh underscores the demanding nature of ATA/JASTA aiding-and-abetting allegations, reinforcing that generalized claims about platform algorithms and ISIS content do not plausibly plead knowing and substantial assistance.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 230(c)(1) bars treating an interactive computer service as the “publisher or speaker” of third-party information, and claims premised on YouTube’s algorithmic sorting and recommendation of user-uploaded ISIS videos still target quintessential publishing functions—organizing, prioritizing, and displaying others’ content at scale. Unlike Roommates.com, where the platform materially contributed to illegality by requiring discriminatory answers and thereby “develop[ing]” unlawful content, the alleged wrong here is the dissemination of ISIS-created material, not content that Google itself required or created. Consistent with Force and Dyroff, recommendations that operate neutrally over third-party content generally fall within § 230 immunity, and extending liability on these pleadings would risk sweeping consequences for ordinary online curation without a clear statutory signal from Congress. Separately, Taamneh underscores the demanding “knowing and substantial assistance” standard for ATA/JASTA aiding-and-abetting liability, and generalized allegations about recommendations and availability of ISIS content do not plausibly clear that hurdle.
